Your AI tutor, set up right.

Each week ends in a closed-book test — no AI, no notes — so it rewards what you can do unaided. The recommended loop: read this week's note yourself, talk through the hard parts and extension prompts with an AI tutor, then check your own understanding on the validation sheet. Here's how to do each step well.

§ 01

Read, discuss, then check yourself

The learning sheet is written to be read on your own; the AI is for the conversation after; the validation sheet is how you confirm it stuck. Keep that order and each piece does its job.

  1. Grab this week's materials

    Open the Materials page, click this week's learning sheet, and download the PDF (the viewer has a download button). Download the validation sheet too once your instructor releases it later in the week.

  2. Read the note through — yourself

    Read the sheet end to end before you open any AI, working the examples on paper as you go, until you have an overall picture of the week. Mark two things as you read: the parts that don't click, and the extension prompts at the end of each part — those are written for discussion, not solo reading. Reading first means you arrive with specific questions instead of a blank stare.

  3. Open an AI tutor and load the sheet

    No install — an AI tutor is just a website. DeepSeek is free and takes PDF uploads (chat.deepseek.com); Claude (claude.ai), ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), Qwen (qwen.ai), and Gemini work too. Make a free account, upload the PDF, and set the ground rules so it acts like a tutor: 

    I've attached this week's linear algebra learning sheet, which
I've already read. Don't dump explanations on me — wait for my
questions, keep answers short, and use a small numeric example
whenever you can. Ready? Ask me which part I want to dig into.
  4. Discuss the hard parts and the extensions

    Bring your marked sticking points first — one concept at a time, using the tricks in §02. Then explore the extension prompts with the AI: they open onto history, applications, "what breaks if…", and links to other weeks. They're for understanding and the mini-lecture, not the closed-book test.

  5. Check yourself on the validation sheet

    Once the week makes sense, the validation sheet is how you verify your own understanding — it practises the same material the test will cover, though not the same questions or difficulty. Work each question yourself, on paper, before checking anything; then compare with the released answer key and use AI only on what you missed. What you can't do here unaided is exactly what to review before the test.

The 10-second self-check

After any AI session, ask yourself: if I closed this chat right now, could I redo this on paper? If not, you watched the AI work — you didn't learn it. Go back and do the step yourself.

§ 02

Six tricks that make it click

These follow the path a new idea takes from huh? to got it — intuition, a worked example, a try of your own, a quick check, then locking it in. Each one asks the AI to make the idea easier, not to drill you. Copy one and swap in this week's topic. One caveat: use them to understand — the actual computing you still do by hand, because that's the muscle the closed-book test checks and the one thing AI can't build for you.

  1. Start with the intuition

    Before symbols, get the plain-English idea and the picture. A concept you can see is far easier to follow into the formulas. 

    Before any formulas, explain in plain English what an eigenvalue
is and why anyone cares, plus the geometric picture. Keep it to a
few sentences — I'll ask for the formal definition after.
  2. Walk a simple example, step by step

    The fastest way in is one small, fully worked case. Ask for the smallest example and have the AI narrate each step and the reason for it. 

    Walk me through the SIMPLEST example of solving A x = b by row
reduction — a 2x2 system — one step at a time. After each step,
say what you did and why, then pause before the next.
  3. Now try a twin — hints, not answers

    Right after a worked example, a near-identical one is easy to attempt — and the attempt is what makes it stick. 

    Give me a similar 2x2 system to solve myself. Let me try each
step; if I'm stuck, give ONE small hint, not the full solution.
Check my answer at the end.
  4. Get a quick, low-stakes check

    A few short questions tell you what you actually have. Asking the AI to re-explain any miss more simply keeps it painless. 

    Ask me 3 quick questions to check I understood this section, one
at a time. If I get one wrong, re-explain that idea more simply
with a tiny example, then ask a similar one.
  5. Lock it in: one line plus a link

    Compress the section to a sentence you could memorize and tie it to something you already know — both make it much easier to recall. 

    Sum up the key idea of this section in one sentence I could
memorize, give me one everyday analogy, and tell me how it
connects to row reduction from an earlier week.
  6. Sanity-check the AI on a tiny case

    Chat models miscount pivots, flip determinant signs, and call a dependent set a basis — fluently, and a longer or more confident answer is no likelier to be right. Two cheap habits catch most of it: check the smallest case, and when it matters, paste the answer into a fresh chat and ask it to find the mistake — a model is bad at auditing its own work. Be most skeptical on anything geometric. 

    Before I trust that, check it on a 2x2 example and recompute the
determinant (or pivot count) a second time. If your two answers
disagree, say so instead of picking one.
More quick tricks
  • Too fast? Say "explain that again like I've never seen it, with a smaller example."
  • Beat the symbols: "read this equation out loud in plain English, term by term."
  • Stay ahead of pitfalls: "which step do students usually get wrong here, and why?"
  • Stuck on a figure? Screenshot it and ask what it's showing about the matrix.
  • Keep a running mistakes note; paste it back and ask for two more practice questions on just those.
§ 03

Frequently asked

Should I read the sheet myself, or just have the AI explain it?

Read it yourself first. The note is built to be read; the AI is for the conversation after — the concepts that didn't click and the extension prompts, which are written for discussion. If you skip the reading and let the AI narrate the sheet, you get the fluent-but-forgettable tour the closed-book test punishes.

Isn't it faster to just ask for the answer?

Faster now, slower where it counts. Copying an answer gets you past one question but leaves nothing you can use when the test changes the numbers — the same studies that show a speed-up on routine problems show roughly a 27% drop on problems that require applying the idea in a new form. The goal isn't to finish the question; it's to be able to redo it with the chat closed.

The AI and the learning sheet disagree — who's right?

The learning sheet and the textbook win. The weekly test is written from them, and large language models hallucinate linear algebra with total confidence — a wrong pivot count, a sign error, a "basis" that isn't independent. When they differ, trust the sheet and settle it yourself on a small example.

How does the validation set differ from the test?

It's how you verify your own understanding once the week's content makes sense — it covers the same scope as the graded closed-book check, though with different questions and difficulty. Work it yourself first, then compare with the released answer key and use AI only on what you missed. It's open-resource where the test is closed-book, so it's an honest self-check: whatever you can't do here unaided is what to review before the test.

Which AI model should I use?

DeepSeek is free, accepts PDF uploads, and is strong on step-by-step reasoning. If you have access, Claude, ChatGPT, and Qwen are strong general-purpose tutors, while Gemini handles the longest chapters. The tricks above work the same in any of them.

How much time, and how often?

A little, often. Several short sessions across the week beat one long cram the night before — spacing is what makes the material stick. Before each test, spend a few minutes letting the AI re-quiz you on earlier weeks too; the gate is rarely about this week alone. And keep it going all term — students who use an AI tutor steadily over months gain far more than those who dip in for a week.

Can I use AI during the test?

No — the weekly test is closed-book: no AI, notes, textbook, or internet. That's the whole design: AI to prepare, you to prove. Everything on this page is about making sure that, when the chat is gone, the skill is still yours.
